title: Explain One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-One, and Many-to-Many relationships in DB design.
shortTitle: Explain One-to-One, One-to-Many, Many-to-One, and Many-to-Many relationships in DB design.
keyPoints: One-to-one means each row on each side relates to at most one row on the other, modeled by a unique foreign key or shared primary key.
One-to-many means one parent row relates to many child rows, modeled by a non-unique foreign key on the child table.
Many-to-one is the same relationship as one-to-many viewed from the child side; the foreign key always lives on the 'many' side.
Many-to-many requires a junction (bridge) table with two foreign keys, one to each side, typically with a composite primary key.
The junction table is the natural place to store relationship attributes like the date a customer acquired a product or a credit limit.
In JPA, these map to `@OneToOne`, `@OneToMany`/`@ManyToOne`, and `@ManyToMany` or an explicit junction entity.
Foreign keys on junction tables and on the many side must be indexed for join performance.

s1_definition.oneliner: One-to-one is a unique foreign key, one-to-many and many-to-one are the two views of a foreign key on the child, and many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **One-to-one** – Each row on each side relates to at most one row on the other, modeled by a shared primary key or a unique foreign key. Used to split sensitive or rarely-used columns.
- **One-to-many / Many-to-one** – One parent relates to many children, modeled by a foreign key on the child side. The two names describe the same link from different perspectives.
- **Many-to-many** – Rows on both sides relate to many rows on the other, modeled with a junction table holding two foreign keys and often a composite primary key.
- **Junction table** – Also called a bridge or associative table, it holds the relationship and any attributes of that relationship, such as a date or status.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, each account has exactly one KYC record and each KYC record belongs to exactly one account: that is one-to-one. One account has many transactions, and each transaction belongs to one account: that is one-to-many from the account side and many-to-one from the transaction side. A customer can hold many products (savings, credit card, loan) and each product type is held by many customers: that is many-to-many, recorded in a separate holdings table pairing customer with product.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Relationship cardinality describes how many rows on one side can associate with rows on the other, and there are three underlying shapes. A one-to-one relationship means each row on each side maps to at most one row on the other. You model it by putting a foreign key on one table that references the other and making it unique, often by letting the child share the parent's primary key. At the National Bank of India, accounts and KYC details are one-to-one with a shared primary key, keeping sensitive KYC data in a separate table with tighter access control.

A one-to-many relationship means one parent relates to many children. You model it by putting a foreign key on the child side referencing the parent's primary key, with no uniqueness so many children share one parent. Many-to-one is not a different mechanism; it is the same relationship viewed from the child. From an account you look one-to-many at its transactions, and from a transaction you look many-to-one at its account. The foreign key lives on the many side either way. This is the most common relationship in any schema.

A many-to-many relationship means both sides can relate to many rows on the other. A single foreign key cannot express it, so you introduce a junction table with one foreign key to each side and a composite primary key. The junction table is also where you store relationship attributes like the date Priya acquired a product or her credit limit on a card. In JPA, a senior engineer should prefer an explicit junction entity over `@ManyToMany` when the junction carries attributes.

The key implementation details are indexing foreign keys on the many side and in junction tables for join performance, choosing cascade behavior deliberately, and solving the N+1 query problem with `JOIN FETCH`.

Remember one sentence: one-to-one is a unique foreign key, one-to-many and many-to-one are the two views of a foreign key on the child, and many-to-many needs a junction table with two foreign keys.
